supplementalRepairs.before: Your Highness holds the duty of the bulwark city—you ought deeply to ponder it.
supplementalRepairs.after: Your Highness holds the responsibility of a bulwark of the ruling house. You should consider this deeply.
supplementalRepairs.reason: 維城 describes a royal kinsman's role as the dynasty's bulwark.

supplementalRepairs.before: At the time Director Wang Min and right aide Guo Bo, because punishments and government were too lenient, debated wishing for harsh regulation. Hong said, "When human feelings are humiliated, a fierce and stern mind arises;
supplementalRepairs.after: At the time, Master of Writing Wang Min and Right Assistant Director Guo Bo considered the administration of punishments too lenient and discussed imposing stricter rules. Hong said, “When people are thwarted and humiliated, a fierce spirit rises in them.
supplementalRepairs.reason: The two offices should be rendered accurately in the parallel literal field; 右丞 specifies the right assistant director.

supplementalRepairs.before: Hong sent Rear General Yao Ping to rescue him; Sheng withdrew.
supplementalRepairs.after: Hong sent Rear General Yao Ping to its relief, and Sheng withdrew.
supplementalRepairs.reason: The threatened place is Qinzhou, not a named male rescuee. Tongjian 117 also has Qin's rear general come to its aid.

supplementalRepairs.before: Yao Shao and General Who Captures Barbarians Yin Zhao, General Who Guards the Army Yao Qia, and others led fifty thousand foot and horse to campaign against Bobo; Yao Hui with ten thousand picked cavalry followed them.
supplementalRepairs.after: Yao Shao, General Who Campaigns against the Enemy Yin Zhao, General Who Guards the Army Yao Qia and others led fifty thousand infantry and cavalry against Bobo. Yao Hui followed with ten thousand picked cavalry.
supplementalRepairs.reason: 征虜 is an expeditionary generalship and does not denote taking captives.

supplementalRepairs.before: Yao Shao advanced and said, "Your Majesty not forgetting to repay virtue—enfeoffing them is right; the ancients respected the affair and charged them with its beginning—it is possible to wait until next spring, then deliberate."
supplementalRepairs.after: Yao Shao stepped forward and said, “Your Majesty remembers to repay virtue; enfeoffing them is right. The ancients treated such matters with reverence and made appointments at the beginning of the year. You could wait until next spring and then consider it.”
supplementalRepairs.reason: The proposed timing in the next clause explains 以始; 'charged them with its beginning' obscures the timing of appointments.

supplementalRepairs.before: Hong sent Colonel of Agile Cavalry Yan Sheng with three thousand horse to hurry there, Martial Guard Yao Yinan leading ten thousand foot soldiers to assist in guarding Luoyang, and also sent General Who Conquers the East and shepherd of Bingzhou Yao Yi to camp south at Shan ford as sounding support.
supplementalRepairs.after: Hong sent Yan Sheng, colonel of the Yue Cavalry, with three thousand horsemen to the rescue. Martial Guard commander Yao Yinan led ten thousand infantry to help defend Luoyang. Hong also sent Yao Yi, General Who Conquers the East and governor of Bingzhou, south to camp at Shan Ford in support.
supplementalRepairs.reason: The parallel literal rendition adds 'agile' and misses that 牧 is a governorship.

supplementalRepairs.before: What will you tell the emperor when he asks where the granaries went?"
supplementalRepairs.after: If the court questions Your Highness, what will you say in reply?”

sourceWitness.excerpt: 若朝廷問殿下者，將何辭以報

supplementalRepairs.reason: The officials ask what Yi can say in reply if the court questions him. The text never says the granary buildings themselves disappeared.

supplementalRepairs.before: Shi Wuhui broke at Stone Pass and ran.
supplementalRepairs.after: Shi Wuhui reached Stone Pass and fled back.
supplementalRepairs.reason: Wuhui reaches the pass and flees back; no fighting or breaking of his formation is stated.

supplementalRepairs.before: Mao Dezu attacked Hongnong Grand Administrator Yin Ya at Li city; the host broke; Dezu sent cavalry pursuing and seized him; afterward he killed the Jin guards and fled to firm Tong Pass.
supplementalRepairs.after: Mao Dezu attacked Yin Ya, governor of Hongnong, at Li city. Ya’s troops broke, and Dezu sent cavalry in pursuit and captured him. Later Ya killed his Jin guards and fled to hold Tong Pass.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 既而殺晉守者奔固潼關

supplementalRepairs.reason: Yin Ya is the captive who later kills his Jin guards and flees to defend the pass; 'firm Tong Pass' obscures the action.

supplementalRepairs.before: No Hedong troops joined Yao Yi; he panicked.
supplementalRepairs.after: No troops from Hedong went over to Yao Yi, and this worried him deeply.
supplementalRepairs.reason: Yi is deeply troubled at the refusal of the Hedong troops; panic is a stronger emotion than 患 here.

supplementalRepairs.before: Hu Yidu objected: "Split the army and one defeat routs every heart—you cannot fight divided."
supplementalRepairs.after: Hu Yidu, one of Shao’s generals, said, “We must concentrate our forces and keep them together. If a detachment suffers a reverse, the men will be seized with fear. How could we fight then?”

sourceWitness.excerpt: 若偏師不利，人心駭懼，胡可以戰

supplementalRepairs.reason: Hu distinguishes the risk to a single detachment from its effect on the whole army's morale.

supplementalRepairs.before: the wicked heir lost his plan, tied cord and surrendered at Zhidao.
supplementalRepairs.after: The wicked heir lost his plan and surrendered with a cord about his neck, as the Qin ruler had at Zhidao.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 凶嗣失圖，系組而降軹道

supplementalRepairs.reason: The appraisal echoes Qin ruler Ziying's surrender in Shiji 6, including the neck cord and Zhidao. Distinguish its allusion from the narrative surrender at the camp gate in s0245.

supplementalRepairs.before: Thus the wheel turns: extremes invite reversal.
supplementalRepairs.after: When things reach their extreme, they reverse course. Is this what the saying means?
supplementalRepairs.reason: The historian closes with a rhetorical question about reversal at extremes; there is no wheel in the source.

supplementalRepairs.before: They sent Hong to Jiankang market and beheaded him; he was thirty years old, on the throne two years.
supplementalRepairs.after: They sent Hong to Jiankang and beheaded him in the marketplace. He was thirty years old and had been on the throne for two years.
supplementalRepairs.reason: The destination is Jiankang; the marketplace is specifically the site of the beheading.

attributionFindings.reason: Preserve both of Yizhi's references and Hedu's co-command. Realign or add English mentions for Hedu and both full-name occurrences, retaining the Chinese spans. Reviewing p143/p164 and p136/p162 as cross-packet duplicates belongs to identity certification.

Remove the spurious explicit Liu Yu English mention m0952; the actual gate is identified by Tongjian 118 as Wang Zhen'e's, while the revised translation leaves it as the Jin camp gate. Preserve the unnamed wife p182 and her Chinese mention m0954, and the existing children summary.

Split m0981 into 仲 for Yizhong p186 and 襄 for Xiang p188, and link both English names. 苻 in this unit is the Fu house: m0978/m0982 may not remain personal links to Fu Jian. Preserve the genuine 舊主/Fu Jian mention and record in s0258. Do not create a Zhongxiang person.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 景茂因仲襄之緒，躡苻亡之會

attributionFindings.reason: The only p192 unit is s0255. Relabel/re-anchor the isolated record as Lei Edi, preserving the Chinese abbreviation and realigning English to Lei Edi. Exclude any Murong Chui canonical anchor. Jinshu 116 and Tongjian 107 identify Lei Edi; p192's chronology must undergo normal independent validation after correction.

Remove the two comparison mentions from s0260 and realign them to s0261 with 楚莊/秦穆. The native title claims in s0261 already establish both titles. The son character inside 子略 belongs to Xing's courtesy name, so it is not independent proof of p193's relationship to p183. The relationship is historically supported by Jinshu 117's opening; hold c1956's source representation for extraction/evidence review without inventing a separate son reference in s0260.

The Qin ruler in Shiji 6 surrendered with the neck cord at Zhidao; the appraisal assimilates Hong's surrender to that precedent. Record the action as historiographical imagery rather than a separate literal relocation. https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/史記/卷006
